explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), prays, “Do not let me be put to shame…” in verse 2. He adds a second request right behind it, that his enemies not exult over him. Two asks in one verse, and not a single wasted word.

Not quite, friend. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), actually prays the opposite in verse 2: “Do not let me be put to shame…” He's asking the LORD to keep him from it. Then he asks that his enemies not exult over him, so he's got two requests packed into one verse.
Verse 3 says the reverse: “Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame…” The word is none, not some and not a few. I think waiting feels a lot lighter when you know that word is in the verse.
Right, friend. David says, “Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame…” None means none. He isn't leaving a little side door open for an exception.

That's the one. Verse 3 says “…those who engage in treachery without cause will be disgraced.” Treachery is betrayal, and the words without cause matter, because this is betrayal that had no reason behind it. David puts that group right next to those who wait for the LORD, and they land in opposite places.

Idols are a fair guess, but this psalm never brings them up. Verse 3 names “…those who engage in treachery without cause…” and says they will be disgraced. That means people who betray without cause. David isn't talking about idols in this verse.

That's a sharp guess, friend, but mocking the poor isn't in this psalm. Verse 3 says “…those who engage in treachery without cause will be disgraced.” Treachery is betrayal, and it's the betrayers David names here. He leaves the poor out of this one.

explanations.answer: The LORD is the God of his salvation
explanations.explanation: Yes! Verse 5 says, “Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation…” David's reason isn't about himself at all. It's about who the LORD is to him. He asks for a guide because he knows whose hand he's holding.

explanations.answer: David has always kept the law
explanations.explanation: David doesn't give that reason in this psalm. In verse 5 he says, “…for You are the God of my salvation…” His ask rests on who the LORD is. He doesn't point to his own record, and later he even asks the LORD to forgive his iniquity (Psalm 25:11).

explanations.answer: David is the one ruling Israel
explanations.explanation: David is the king (2 Samuel 5:3), but that's not the reason he gives here. Verse 5 says, “…for You are the God of my salvation…” Notice he doesn't bring up his title at all. When he asks to be taught, he comes as someone who needs the LORD, not as the one in charge.
Yes, friend. Verse 5 says, “all day long I wait for You.” That's the whole day spent waiting. I'd be checking my oven timer every two minutes.
Night is a fair guess, since waiting does feel longer in the dark. But verse 5 says “all day long I wait for You.” The word is day. David's whole day is spent waiting on the LORD.

A year would be some serious waiting. But verse 5 says, “all day long I wait for You.” The word is day, so the waiting fills his whole day. I think that makes it sound like something you could actually do.

explanations.answer: The LORD's compassion and loving devotion
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 6 says, “Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age.” David isn't handing the LORD a list of things he's done. He's pointing at what the LORD is like, and says it lasts from age to age.

That would be one way to make a case, but it's not what David does. Verse 6 says, “Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and loving devotion, for they are from age to age.” His eyes are on the LORD's character, not his own wins.

David doesn't mention offerings here. In verse 6 he asks the LORD to remember His “…compassion and loving devotion…” and he says they are from age to age. The whole request is about the LORD, not about anything David brought.

It's actually the other way around, friend. Verse 7 says, “Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts…” He asks the LORD not to remember them. I think that's a man who wants a clean counter, not a pile of old crumbs on it.

Yes! Verse 7 has David asking, “Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts…” So he asks the LORD not to remember them. Then he asks to be remembered according to the LORD's loving devotion instead.

That's the word. Verse 8 says, “Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way.” Read that slowly. The LORD's goodness is the reason He shows sinners the way. I'd say that's good news for every one of us who's ever had a rough batch.

Scholars would fit a fancy lecture hall, but verse 8 says something else. It reads, “Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way.” The word is sinners. David doesn't say you need a degree for the LORD to show you the way.

Priests are a reasonable guess, but they aren't in this verse. Verse 8 says, “Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way.” The one who gets shown is the sinner. No special title is listed.
Yes, friend. Verse 9 says, “He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way.” Notice there are two parts there, guiding and teaching. It's the LORD doing both.

It's true, actually, baker. Verse 9 says, “He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way.” Most folks hand you a map and wish you luck. Here the humble get the guiding AND the teaching.

explanations.answer: Those who keep His covenant and decrees
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Verse 10 says, “All the LORD’s ways are loving and faithful to those who keep His covenant and His decrees.” Loving AND faithful, both at once. You know that friend who's super sweet but never shows up? Not the same thing, and David names exactly who gets both.

explanations.answer: Those who dwell within His holy city
explanations.explanation: A holy city sounds right, but verse 10 doesn't mention one. It says the LORD's ways are loving and faithful “…to those who keep His covenant and His decrees.” The ones named are the covenant keepers, not a place on a map.

explanations.answer: Those who offer Him daily sacrifices
explanations.explanation: Sacrifices are a natural guess, but they don't appear in this verse. Verse 10 says the LORD's ways are loving and faithful “…to those who keep His covenant and His decrees.” That's who David names.

David actually says the opposite. Verse 11 reads, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity, for it is great.” He doesn't shrink it down to a crumb. I think that kind of honesty is a big part of why this psalm lands.

Yes, friend. In verse 11 David says, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity, for it is great.” He calls it great, with no dressing it up. And he asks for forgiveness anyway, for the sake of the LORD's name.

explanations.answer: Instruct him in the path chosen for him
explanations.explanation: Yes! Verse 12 says, “Who is the man who fears the LORD? He will instruct him in the path chosen for him.” So the LORD does the teaching, and there's a path chosen for that man. That's a whole lot better than winging it and hoping for the best.

explanations.answer: Give him a crown and a throne
explanations.explanation: David is a king (2 Samuel 5:3), so it's an easy guess, but verse 12 doesn't say this. It says the LORD “…will instruct him in the path chosen for him.” The promise there is instruction, not a throne.

explanations.answer: Keep every trouble far away from him
explanations.explanation: That sounds nice, but it's not what verse 12 says. It says the LORD “…will instruct him in the path chosen for him.” And David himself says later, “The troubles of my heart increase…” (Psalm 25:17), so the psalm isn't promising a trouble-free road.

That's the word. Verse 13 says, “His soul will dwell in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land.” So it reaches past the man himself, on to his descendants. That's a blessing with a long line behind it.

That would be a plot twist, but verse 13 goes a different way. It says, “His soul will dwell in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land.” The ones inheriting the land are his descendants. David's enemies show up later in the psalm, in a very different spot.
Servants don't show up in verse 13. It says, “His soul will dwell in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land.” The word is descendants, meaning the man's own line coming after him.

Yes, friend. Verse 15 says, “My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh.” That little word for gives the reason. David looks to the LORD because of what he says the LORD will do.

It's true, actually. Verse 15 says, “My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh.” The word for ties the two parts together. His eyes stay on the LORD because he says the LORD will free his feet.

That's right. Verse 16 says, “Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted.” David gives no fancy reason, just where he is. I think it takes some courage to say lonely out loud to the LORD.
A palace isn't mentioned here at all. Verse 16 says, “Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted.” The reason David gives is how he feels and where he is, not anything he lost.
Crops don't come up anywhere in this psalm. Verse 16 says, “Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted.” That's David's reason, lonely and afflicted, said straight to the LORD.

It goes the other direction, friend. Verse 17 says, “The troubles of my heart increase…” They're growing, not shrinking. I think this one hurts, and David asks the LORD to free him from his distress right after.
Yes. Verse 17 says, “The troubles of my heart increase; free me from my distress.” They're growing, not shrinking. I think this is a heavy spot in the psalm, and David doesn't hide it.

That's the word. Verse 18 says, “Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins.” Notice it's all my sins, and it comes right alongside his trouble. David brings the whole load at once.

Doubts are a fair thing to bring to the LORD, but they aren't in this verse. Verse 18 says, “Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins.” The word is sins, and David asks for all of them to be taken away.
Tears would fit the mood, but verse 18 uses a different word. It says, “Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins.” David asks for his sins to be taken away, all of them.
That's backwards, friend. Verse 19 says, “Consider my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with vicious hatred.” Many, not few. David brings it straight to the LORD.
Yes. Verse 19 says, “Consider my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with vicious hatred.” So they're many, not a few. David gives it to the LORD straight, which I think takes some courage.

explanations.answer: He takes refuge in the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's right. Verse 20 says, “Guard my soul and deliver me; let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in You.” His reason is where he runs to, not what he's done. It's a short sentence with a lot of room in it.

David doesn't say that here. Verse 20 gives this reason: “…for I take refuge in You.” He has also already asked the LORD to take away all his sins (Psalm 25:18), so he's not claiming a spotless record.

explanations.answer: He built the LORD a temple
explanations.explanation: A temple doesn't come up in this psalm. Verse 20 gives a different reason: “…for I take refuge in You.” David's ask rests on trusting the LORD, not on anything he built.

Yes, friend. Verse 21 says, “May integrity and uprightness preserve me, because I wait for You.” He asks for integrity and uprightness to preserve him, and he gives his waiting on the LORD as the reason. Waiting and integrity in one breath, and I bet that's not easy to hold together.
It's true, actually. Verse 21 says, “May integrity and uprightness preserve me, because I wait for You.” David asks for them to preserve him. And he ties it right back to his waiting on the LORD.

That's it. The very last line, verse 22, says, “Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress.” After all that talk of his own trouble, David ends with a prayer for the whole people. That's a big finish.
Egypt never shows up in this psalm. The last line, verse 22, says, “Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress.” That's the name David closes with, Israel.
Assyria isn't named anywhere in this psalm. The last line, verse 22, says, “Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress.” David ends by praying for Israel.
